storyboard.addedInformation: The clock makes the peak a dated deadline on the body, not a dollar number on a chart.
storyboard.claim: Peak net worth is a biological date, not a financial number.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman studying a clock: the peak is a date on the calendar of the body.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the crest-and-fall curve from 119 by naming what sets the crest: biology.

storyboard.addedInformation: Reframes the goal from a dollar target to an age, answering the $2 million question directly.
storyboard.claim: The target is a specific age, not a specific fortune.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host answering the $2 million question: it is an age you hit, not a number.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question 120 raises: no fixed dollar figure, a fixed stage of life.

storyboard.addedInformation: Perkins as the calculator pins the window to 45-60, grounding the abstraction in actuarial data.
storyboard.claim: Perkins calculates the peak window as ages 45 to 60.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Perkins presenting his notes: the peak window is 45 to 60.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Puts numbers on 121's age-peak: the actuarial window.

storyboard.addedInformation: The slumped body shows why the window closes: after 60 the vessel cannot convert money into joy.
storyboard.claim: After 60, declining health restricts how much money can be enjoyed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman slumped, worried: the body that sets the spending limit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the 45-60 window: the body behind the math.

storyboard.addedInformation: A concrete timestamped scene: 58, home office, coffee, laptop — the life the listener pictures themselves in.
storyboard.claim: Picture yourself at 58, coffee in hand, checking the brokerage account.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman at 58 in his home office, coffee cup in hand, laptop open.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: New scene: from the abstract window to a lived moment inside it.

storyboard.addedInformation: The coin and the brief happy rush show the dopamine of the number ticking up — before the window view undercuts it.
storyboard.claim: The 2.5 million rush curdles: the body vetoes the balance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman slumped before the giant coin: 2.5 million and dusty golf clubs, the triumph curdled.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same office, same morning: the dopamine hit of the number.

storyboard.addedInformation: The same man deflated: maximum account power beside a body that cannot deploy it, golf clubs dusty.
storyboard.claim: The account is at maximum power but the body can no longer deploy it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman slumped and sad: the shot spine beside the dusty clubs.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The turn on 125's rush: the body vetoes the balance.

storyboard.addedInformation: Rejects the high-score reading: net worth is fuel for dated experiences, not points.
storyboard.claim: Net worth is a tool to fund your calendar, not a video-game high score.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host pointing at a calendar: money as fuel for dated plans.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Draws the lesson from the golfer: the tool, not the trophy.

storyboard.addedInformation: The shield names the protected floor: basic living plus medical until death, calculated, not guessed.
storyboard.claim: Once the calculated survival threshold is covered, the floor is protected.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman thinking beside the shield: the protected survival floor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines the line where funding the calendar ends and hoarding begins.

storyboard.addedInformation: The strike marks surplus hoarding as rejected: declining health blocks converting extra money into joy.
storyboard.claim: Hoarding past the threshold buys abstract numbers, not experiences.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman idle and sad before struck-through numbers: surplus that converts to nothing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The verdict on surplus: numbers the body cannot spend.

storyboard.addedInformation: A named case study enters: the billionaire who proves psychology beats math.
storyboard.claim: John Arnold, the billionaire, is the case study of the psychology.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Arnold introduced in his suit: wealth that could not break the habit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: New face: from the abstract hoarder to the named billionaire.

storyboard.addedInformation: The promise staged between the two men: $15 million meant quitting, said to Perkins himself.
storyboard.claim: Perkins quotes Arnold promise to quit at fifteen million.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Perkins retelling Arnold vow across the desk: fifteen million and I am done, a promise quoted not a joint exit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Arnold's own exit line, quoted back at him.

storyboard.addedInformation: The dare plus the answer: he never walked away — the vow staged as already broken.
storyboard.claim: He vowed a punch if he kept trading — and he kept trading.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Arnold bracing, worried: the dare he lost, still at the desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The dare attached to the promise: asked and answered, he stayed.

storyboard.addedInformation: The scale of the miss: 38 years old, billions past the exit line.
storyboard.claim: He quit at 38 with over $4 billion, not $15 million.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Arnold buried behind towering coin stacks at 38: the accumulation trap.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The punchline number against the $15 million vow.

storyboard.addedInformation: Names the mechanism: the ultimate example, billion-B included, of the trap.
storyboard.claim: This is the ultimate accumulation trap.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host naming it: even billions did not spring the trap.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Labels what Arnold just demonstrated.

storyboard.addedInformation: The target keeps moving downfield as he walks: 15 became 100 became a billion, the wired-in treadmill.
storyboard.claim: Even a billionaire stays on the treadmill as the goalposts recede.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Arnold walking toward a target that keeps sliding away.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalizes Arnold: the receding goalposts behind every balance.

storyboard.addedInformation: The escalation chain as structure: each target causes the next, and the brain never switches to de-accumulation.
storyboard.claim: $15 million became $100 million became a billion: the brain acquires, never de-accumulates.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-step flow: $15M flowing into $100M flowing into $4B.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Diagrams 135's receding goalposts as a causal chain.

storyboard.addedInformation: The devil's advocate case staged sincerely: what if the dealing itself is the joy?
storyboard.claim: What if he just likes working — the deal is his joy?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Arnold lit up at the desk: the thrill of the trade as fulfillment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pushback on the trap verdict: the work-as-joy defense.

storyboard.addedInformation: Steel-mans the defense: intellectual combat and outsmarting the market as genuine fulfillment.
storyboard.claim: The thrill of the deal is his fulfillment — the common ultra-wealthy defense.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Arnold celebrating a won trade: combat, wit, victory.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the defense: why should he quit what fulfills him?

storyboard.addedInformation: Perkins concedes the premise head on: if work genuinely satisfies, that is fantastic — play on.
storyboard.claim: Perkins agrees: if work genuinely satisfies, play the game.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Perkins answering directly: satisfaction from working is a fine game.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Perkins takes the defense seriously before redirecting it.

storyboard.addedInformation: The sawdust analogy: earnings are shavings off the carving, not the carving.
storyboard.claim: The money is merely a byproduct, sawdust from the carving.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Perkins carving wood while sawdust piles below: the byproduct, not the point.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes the defense: keep the game, reprice the winnings.

storyboard.addedInformation: The rejected behavior struck through: unspent surplus is extra lives discarded.
storyboard.claim: Keeping the surplus unspent throws away the extra lives earned.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman watching earned lives slip away unclaimed: winnings never spent.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The cost of sawdust worship: lives left on the table.

storyboard.addedInformation: The grave literalizes the verdict: loving the job does not excuse dying with potential unspent.
storyboard.claim: Dying with billions unspent wastes the energy, whatever you loved.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A grave on the dusk hill: billions carried down unspent.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The endpoint of 141's waste: the energy dies with its holder.

storyboard.addedInformation: The unlived alternative: hospitals, schools, a world tour — the gift reaching outward instead of dying in the bank.
storyboard.claim: Unspent money could have funded hospitals, schools, a family world tour.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman reaching out with the gift: the tour, the schools, the wards that never were.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Itemizes what the grave in 142 swallowed.

storyboard.addedInformation: The hourglass literalizes the closing window: convert money into memory while sand remains.
storyboard.claim: Find your peak and convert money into memory before the window closes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman studying the hourglass: sand left for converting money into memory.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from the waste to the instruction: convert before closing.

storyboard.addedInformation: The freeze named: one primal emotion blocks the math everyone just accepted.
storyboard.claim: One primal emotion freezes us: fear.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman frozen, worried: the single emotion behind the freeze.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Asks the hard question 144 leaves: why is the clear math so hard?

storyboard.addedInformation: Names the next concept: terror of the unknown has a price, and we are overpaying it.
storyboard.claim: This brings us to pricing fear: terror of the unknown.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host introducing the ledger: fear with a price tag.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Bridges fear to economics: the price tag comes next.

storyboard.addedInformation: The doomsday-prepper grip literalized: a wallet clutched against running out of breath with money left.
storyboard.claim: Precautionary saving: hoarding cash, terrified of outliving money.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman clutching the wallet: the prepper hoard against the unknown.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines the behavior pricing fear will judge: the hoard.

storyboard.addedInformation: The shield repriced: oversaving is protection bought at a brutal irrational markup.
storyboard.claim: Oversaving is insurance bought at a brutal markup.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman weighing the shield: protection priced far above value.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Perkins prices the hoard: protection at a markup.

storyboard.addedInformation: The scale literalized: localized fear of broke on one pan, certain biological expiry on the other.
storyboard.claim: We price the fear of running out of money against the certainty of running out of time.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host at the balance: fear weighed against certain time.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the markup's math: the two pans being weighed.

storyboard.addedInformation: The terrifying image landed literally: IV tubes, beeping monitor, $200,000 for weeks of ceiling tiles.
storyboard.claim: Imagine spending your last $200,000 on weeks in a hospital bed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman in the sterile bed, tubes taped, monitor beeping: the last $200,000 draining.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Makes the markup visceral: the bed the over-insurance buys.

storyboard.addedInformation: Tighter on the same bed: incapacitated, staring at beige tile — what the money actually purchases.
storyboard.claim: Three extra weeks staring at a ceiling tile, incapacitated.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Close on Everyman's stare at the beige tile: three purchased weeks of nothing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same bed, tighter: the purchase itemized.

storyboard.addedInformation: The design question: the point where protection flips into theft.
storyboard.claim: When does caution stop protecting and start robbing you?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A hoarder clutching his wallet while coins slip through: caution tipping into robbery.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the haunting bed into a design question.

storyboard.addedInformation: The trade staged: vibrant capable years ground through stressful weeks to hyperinsure a bedridden 95.
storyboard.claim: You trade vibrant 50s grinding 60-hour weeks to hyperinsure a bedridden 95.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman trudging through the office grind: healthy years traded for a bed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers 152's question with the concrete trade being made.

storyboard.addedInformation: The 95-year-old self staged as an ordinary older woman who statistically may never arrive.
storyboard.claim: That 95-year-old self statistically might not even exist.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An older woman sitting quietly: the future self being over-insured.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Undercuts 153's trade: the beneficiary may never exist.

storyboard.addedInformation: The mechanical exit from fear: annuities cover the survival threshold so life energy is not the insurance.
storyboard.claim: Perkins offers annuities to cover the survival threshold.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Perkins pointing to the mechanism: the annuity covering the floor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The solution after the diagnosis: a mechanism, not more hoarding.

storyboard.addedInformation: The rejected just-in-case million struck through: hoarding for a miraculous 104.
storyboard.claim: Don't hoard an extra million just in case you live to 104.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman clutching the wallet under a struck verdict: the just-in-case million rejected.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names what the annuity replaces: the just-in-case million.

storyboard.addedInformation: The handoff literalized: cash to the insurer, guaranteed monthly payout back until death — longevity risk transferred.
storyboard.claim: Hand the insurer cash; they guarantee payouts until death, killing longevity risk.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman handing the coin across to the suited insurer: cash out, lifetime payouts back.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the mechanism: the exchange that ends the hoard.

storyboard.addedInformation: The crude self-insurance rejected: your own life energy is the worst policy.
storyboard.claim: Don't use your precious life energy as crude DIY insurance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman pointing away the struck DIY policy: transfer the risk instead.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The moral of the exchange: stop self-insuring with your life.

storyboard.addedInformation: Every tangible fear insurable — house, car, longevity — staged at the protected home with shield in hand.
storyboard.claim: There is an insurance product for every tangible fear: house, car, outliving money.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman holding the shield before the house: every tangible fear covered.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Widens the mechanism: every fear but one has a policy — time comes next.
